t: 2763. Sum of Imbalance Numbers of All Subarrays
o: The imbalance number counts adjacent gaps > 1 in the sorted subarray. With n ≤ 1000 there are ~500k subarrays, so an O(n²) enumeration with O(1) incremental updates per extension is the intended complexity. Key observation: fixing the left endpoint and extending right, the imbalance count only changes when the newly added value v is 'new' (not already present): if both v−1 and v+1 are present, v bridges a gap (count decreases by 1); if neither neighbor is present, v creates a gap (count increases by 1); otherwise unchanged. Example 2 confirms: extending [1,3] with another 3 changes nothing, but adding 5 to [1,3,3,3] raises imbalance from 1 to 2.
k: Fix the left endpoint and extend rightward, updating the imbalance count incrementally in O(1).
Only genuinely new values change the count: bridging two existing neighbors removes a gap; isolated insertion adds one.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate Left Endpoint with Presence Array
a.i: For each left index i, keep a boolean presence array over values 1..n and a running imbalance counter. Extending to j, if nums[j] was unseen, adjust the counter based on whether v−1/v+1 are present, then add the counter to the answer.
s: For each i, clear/reset the presence array and counter.
For each j ≥ i: if v = nums[j] unseen, decrement counter if both neighbors present, increment if neither present (and j > i), mark seen.
Add counter to the global answer after each extension.
a.t: O(n²) — nested loops over subarray endpoints with O(1) updates
a.sp: O(n) — the presence array reused per left endpoint

w: An O(n log n) contribution technique exists (counting each element's effect as a left/right boundary using monotonic stacks or sorted insertion), but O(n²) suffices for n ≤ 1000 and is far less error-prone. Pitfalls: duplicates must not change the count (hence the `if not seen[v]` guard), and the very first element of a subarray must not create a gap (the `j > i` guard). Test with all-equal arrays (answer 0) and strictly increasing arrays.
